newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: CHURCH CALLS FOR NO FUNDING FOR CLONING
The New South Wales Council of Churches has called on the Prime Minister to give a guarantee that not a cent of government money will be used in experiments involving the cloning of human beings.

The council's Rev Wayne Magee says he wants John Howard to follow President Clinton's lead and give Australians an unshakeable assurance that no government funds will be allocated for such experimentation.

Mr Magee says the federal, state and territory governments must meet as soon as possible to discuss the establishment of national guidelines to control genetic engineering, in particular, the cloning of humans.
SENATE APPROVES TWO NEW CASA BOARD POSITIONS
The Senate has approved Federal Transport Minister John Sharp's bid to appoint new Directors to the Civil Aviation Safety Authority.
It's a significant win for the Minister, who's repeatedly called for the Board's resignation, claiming it lacks suitable aviation experience.
The Directors, including Chairman Justice Bill Fisher, have consistently refused, strongly defending their credentials.
Mr Sharp has now moved to effectively reduce their influence, with the Senate last night passing a bill that creates two new Board positions.
He's expected to appoint the new directors within weeks.
DODSON SAYS PM A SPECTATOR ON WIK
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Social Justice Commissioner, Mick Dodson, says the Prime Minister should be doing more in relation to the High Court Wik judgement.
The government is expected to respond to the judgement, which found that native title and pastoral leases can co-exist, by Easter.
But Mr Dodson's accused John Howard of being a "spectator", and not criticising "hysterical" debate.
He says most of the debate has been regretable, and believes the Prime Minister should have pulled up those who've called for native title to be extinguished.
Indigenous representatives will today meet with the National Farmers Federation in Canberra.
BLACKHAWK INQUIRY REPORT TO BE RELEASED TOMORROW
The results of the Blackhawk Inquiry will be released today in Canberra, and will coincide with releases in Perth and Townsville for the families of those killed and the officers involved.
18 soldiers -- 15 from the Special Air Service and 3 from the fifth Aviation unit -- were killed when two Blackhawk helicopters collided mid-air on a counter-terrorism exercise in June last year.
It was the army's worst peacetime disaster.
The Board of Inquiry, which finalised its report in December at a cost of nearly two-and-a-half-million dollars, is expected to recommend disciplinary action against three officers.
MARATHON TALKS TO AVOID GP STRIKE
Marathon talks are continuing to try to avert a public transport workers strike in Melbourne this weekend.
Despite a new Government offer, four hours of negiotiations with the Public transport union failed failed to break the deadlock earlier today.
Union secretary Peter Bourke says, at this stage, the strike on Saturday and Sunday is still on.
Transport Minister Robin Cooper says the new offer is fair, and the union should accept it, but he's not confident it will.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
